Second, the norms check: a second crew rarely doubles output — access, crane time and a congested work-face eat into it. Give me the steel quantities and I'll test the split against the productivity KB rather than assume one plus one is two.

questions.q: How many days from a 6-day week vs a night shift, and do I need to change the P6 calendar first?
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, Calendar Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Compares calendar-based levers and confirms the calendar supports the extra time.
questions.answer_full: On the jetty, the night shift is worth about +6 wd in the F9 model — the strongest calendar lever I've tested. A 6-day week I'd expect to land a bit lower, but I have to model it, not quote it. The key point: both only compute if you edit the P6 calendar first — the activities must sit on a 6-day or shift calendar or F9 won't see the extra hours and you'll accelerate on paper only. Change the calendar, then re-run.

questions.q: Can I fast-track by overlapping engineering/procurement with construction, and is the re-sequence actually constructable?
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, Constructability Review
questions.answer_sketch: Models phase overlap and surfaces the OOS/buildability risk it creates.
questions.answer_full: Here's the catch: engineering and procurement are broadly on track — the delay is site execution at the jetty. Overlapping E/P won't move a finish driven by pile driving and deck works, so fast-tracking the front end buys little here. Where overlap does help downstream I'll model it, but the constructability review has to clear it first — you already carry 12 out-of-sequence activities, and forcing more overlap risks turning a paper gain into rework. Fix the jetty; don't re-sequence the office.

questions.q: If I crash this activity, does it just shove the delay downstream, and where does the critical path jump next?
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Confirms local acceleration removes the bottleneck rather than relocating it, and names the new controlling path.
questions.answer_full: Good instinct — that's exactly the trap. On this job, crash the jetty enough and the path jumps to Silo Structure: it's only about 9 wd behind at TF −9, so it takes over quickly. That's why I never accelerate one front in isolation. When I run the what-if I look at where the next controlling chain appears after each cut, so you're not spending money moving the bottleneck instead of removing it. Name the activity and I'll show you where the path lands next.

questions.q: How many days can I recover before I hit a resource ceiling or overtime fatigue stops helping?
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Finds the point of diminishing returns and the maximum realistic recovery.
questions.answer_full: Straight answer: the schedule models the time gain, but the ceiling itself is partly a judgment call the plan can only half-ground. The what-if shows diminishing returns — a second piling crew adds about +4 wd, a third would add less as the work-face congests — and Productivity Intelligence flags where implied output beats the norms. But sustained overtime fatigue and the real crew cap are site knowledge. Give me the manpower limit you can genuinely hold and I'll find where extra hours stop paying.

questions.q: Show me a resourced recovery scenario that hits the milestone, and check the resulting manpower peak is staffable.
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, Critical Path Analyzer, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: A concrete recovery plan with its manpower peak tested against realistic staffing.
questions.answer_full: I can build it, but be clear on the honest limit: manpower here is man-hours, not headcount, so the peak I test is an hours curve, not a body count. The scenario I'd assemble is jetty night shift (+6) plus second piling crew (+4) stacked on the governing path, then re-run F9 on the 47-day gap — and it won't fully close, so we'll add silo measures. I'll flag where the man-hour peak spikes against norms; converting that to bodies is your call with the CM.

questions.q: Rank my recovery options best-to-worst by days recovered per dollar, and what does acceleration do to CPI?
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, EVM, Reporting Studio
questions.answer_sketch: A prioritized acceleration menu with the cost-efficiency hit for the go/no-go call.
questions.answer_full: I can rank by days recovered — night shift about +6 wd, second piling crew about +4 — and the schedule is cost-loaded, so I can show the discipline budgets. But true days-per-dollar needs each lever's crash cost, which isn't in the P6 file; keep the cost side qualitative until you feed me rates. On CPI: you're at 0.94 already, and acceleration — overtime, extra crews — burns cost faster than value, so expect it to dip further. That's the trade you're buying the time with.

questions.q: Just find me the cheapest crash plan automatically — which activities and by how much to hit the date at least cost.
questions.grounds: GAP — manual what-ifs only, no time-cost optimization
questions.answer_sketch: Not groundable: least-cost crash optimization across the network isn't implemented.
questions.answer_full: I can't ground that one yet. The tool runs manual what-ifs — it doesn't do least-cost crash optimisation across the network; the classic time-cost trade-off algorithm isn't built. What I can do today is rank the driving activities by finish sensitivity and test levers one at a time, which gets you close to a least-effort plan by hand. A true automatic cheapest-crash needs crash-cost-per-day loaded on every activity plus the optimiser — not there. I won't hand you a number I haven't actually computed.

questions.q: Can I realistically source the extra crews and equipment in this market, and by when?
questions.grounds: GAP — labour/plant market data outside the schedule
questions.answer_sketch: Not groundable: local resource availability is human judgment the plan can't ground.
questions.answer_full: That's outside what the schedule can answer — labour and plant market availability isn't in the P6 file, so anything I gave you would be a guess. The model can tell you how many man-hours and which trades a recovery needs, and by when they'd have to be on site to bite. But whether the local market can deliver a second piling crew and a rig by that date is your procurement and CM call. Tell me what you can realistically source and I'll test it in F9.

catalog.blurb: The next few weeks up close — what has already slipped in this window, what is ready to start, and what protects the date now.

questions.q: Which activities were due to start or finish by this data date but haven't — what has quietly slipped in the current window before it reaches the critical path?

questions.answer_sketch: Time-status view of overdue starts/finishes — the earliest slip signal, caught before it hits the driving path.
questions.answer_full: Treat this as your early-warning list, not a status read. Pull the Update Analysis time-status view off the 19 Jul data date — every activity that was due to start or finish and hasn't. Two rules: chase the jetty fronts first, since pile-driving and deck are already the -18 wd driver baked into your +47 wd; and watch Silo Structure hardest at TF -9, because an overdue start there is what turns it critical. Clear these this week, before the slip migrates onto the driving path and hardens.

questions.q: What is blocking my imminent work — which upcoming activities have incomplete predecessors or unmet constraints and are not ready to start?
questions.grounds: Update Analysis, Critical Path Analyzer, Schedule Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Readiness / constraint-clearing check on near-term activities, driven off logic and the driving-path work-fronts — the core of weekly work-front management.
questions.answer_full: This is your weekly work-front management. Run the readiness check — near-term activities whose predecessors aren't finished or whose constraints aren't cleared — so you don't push crews to a front that isn't ready. Prioritise the jetty: fender install can't start until deck completes, and deck is trailing pile-driving. Bear in mind the 12 out-of-sequence activities and 3 open ends can make a front look 'ready' when it isn't. Resolve the real blockers — access, free-issue, predecessor completion — a week ahead, not on the morning of.

questions.q: Give me a three-week look-ahead — what's starting and finishing on the driving path?
questions.grounds: Update Analysis, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Upcoming activities and active driving fronts for the near window.
questions.answer_full: I'll filter the look-ahead to what governs the date, not the whole 1,503-line list. The next three weeks are dominated by the Marine & Jetty chain — pile-driving into deck into fender install — at TF -18 and driving your +47 wd late finish (forecast ~20 Apr 2027). Silo Structure sits just behind at TF -9; treat it as the second front to protect, because it flips critical if the jetty slips further. Use this as your look-ahead spine and hang the recovery levers off it — jetty night shift ~+6 wd, second piling crew ~+4 wd.

catalog.blurb: DCMA logic quality, the specific defects, whether the update was even statused honestly, and a corrected file to reimport.

questions.q: Does my schedule pass the DCMA 14-point check — what's my overall score?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: One headline pass/fail read across all 14 metrics.
questions.answer_full: The Health Review runs all 14 points and this file reads clean overall — nothing structural is corrupting the numbers. Across 1,503 activities the only real flags are 3 open ends and 12 out-of-sequence activities, both modest and neither manufacturing the delay. I'd treat the schedule as reliable enough to report and forecast off. Tidy those two items before resubmission, but don't let anyone dismiss the +47-working-day slip as a data artefact — it's genuine, driven by the jetty.

questions.q: Which of the 14 checks am I failing, and by how much am I over threshold?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Ranked failing checks with actual vs allowed percentage.
questions.answer_full: Two points stand out. Logic completeness catches the 3 open ends — activities with no successor, so their slip doesn't drive the finish. Out-of-sequence flags 12 activities progressed against their logic. On 1,503 activities both sit low against the DCMA thresholds, so we're marginal, not failing wholesale. Read the exact percentages off the Health Review, but the action list is short: tie in the 3 open ends and reconcile the 12 OOS items. Everything else is within tolerance.

questions.q: Give me a plain-English summary of how healthy the logic actually is.
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Non-planner narrative of logic quality for briefing the client.
questions.answer_full: In plain terms the skeleton is sound. Out of 1,503 activities only 3 have loose ends and 12 were ticked off out of their planned order — housekeeping, not rot. Crucially, the delay is real, not a logic or lag trick, so when we tell the client we're +47 working days late driven by the jetty, that number holds up. I'd brief them the schedule is trustworthy for decisions once we close the open ends. No structural red flags.

questions.q: Is this clean enough to submit to the consultant, or will they bounce it — and for what?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review, Constructability Review
questions.answer_sketch: Go/no-go flagging the issues reviewers typically reject a schedule for.
questions.answer_full: Close, but tidy it first. A sharp reviewer bounces on the 3 open ends every time — every activity bar the last milestone needs a successor — and they'll query the 12 out-of-sequence items and want a status note on each. None of that is fatal; it's half a day of housekeeping. Close them, confirm no dangling milestones, and it clears review. Submitting as-is invites a rejection over cosmetics while the real story — a genuine 47-day jetty slip — gets buried.

questions.q: Was this update statused correctly before I trust the numbers — activities in progress with no actual start, completed work with no actual dates, remaining duration on finished activities, or a stale data date?
questions.grounds: Update Analysis, Schedule Audit, Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Honest data-entry quality check on the update (distinct from the forensic back-dating question) — validate before reporting any EVM or delay figure, since garbage-in undermines every downstream number.
questions.answer_full: Validate this before you trust any EVM or delay figure — garbage in, garbage out. The Update Analysis checks the classic tells: progress with no actual start, completed work missing actual dates, remaining duration left on finished activities. Data date is current at 19 Jul 2026, so no stale-date distortion. The 12 out-of-sequence items are the main statusing flag to reconcile. Clear those and the SPI 0.66 / +47-day read stands on solid data. Never report numbers off an unvalidated update.

questions.q: Show me every dangling activity and open end, and why each is a problem.
questions.grounds: Schedule Audit, Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Itemized dangling/open-end list with a reason per item.
questions.answer_full: The audit lists all 3 open ends by ID with a reason for each. An activity with no successor (open finish) can slip freely without pushing the finish — so it hides delay; a missing predecessor (open start) lets it drift with no driver. On a 1,503-activity network 3 is low, but every one distorts float and the critical-path calculation. Close them and your negative-float picture — the jetty at TF -18, silo at TF -9 — becomes fully trustworthy.

questions.q: Suggest the missing links to close my open ends and give me a corrected XER.
questions.grounds: Schedule Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Evidence-based predecessor/successor suggestions plus a downloadable corrected file.
questions.answer_full: The audit proposes evidence-based predecessors/successors for each of the 3 open ends — inferred from WBS neighbours, activity codes, naming and construction sequence, ranked by confidence — then lets you accept or edit before it writes a corrected XER to reimport into P6. Treat them as suggestions, not gospel: eyeball each against how the work actually builds, especially anything tying into the jetty path. Never auto-apply logic to a live baseline without a planner's eye on it first.

questions.q: How many hard constraints, where are they, and am I over the DCMA 5% limit?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Constraint count and placement against the DCMA threshold.
questions.answer_full: The Health Review counts every constraint, flags the hard ones (Must-Finish-On, Mandatory) and tests the total against DCMA's 5% ceiling — read the exact figure off the report. What matters here: the +47-day slip is genuine, so no one has bolted a Must-Finish-On the completion milestone to mask negative float — that's the manipulation to watch for. If any hard constraint sits on the jetty or silo path, strip it; you want TF -18 showing honestly, not suppressed.

questions.q: How much of my logic is Finish-to-Start versus other types — too many SS/FF/SF to convert?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: FS/SS/FF/SF mix against the DCMA >90% FS guidance.
questions.answer_full: The Health Review gives the FS/SS/FF/SF split against DCMA's >90%-FS guidance — pull the exact mix off the report. As a rule, heavy SS/FF is where overlap gets hidden and logic goes soft. If the jetty chain (pile-drive → deck → fender) is threaded with start-to-starts rather than clean finish-to-starts, that overlap may be flattering the durations. Convert what you can to FS, but not blindly — some marine overlap is genuine, so keep the links that reflect how the work truly runs.

questions.q: How many lags and leads do I have, are any excessive, and are they justified or hiding real work?
questions.grounds: Schedule Audit, Schedule Health Review, Constructability Review
questions.answer_sketch: Lag/lead counts against DCMA, negative-lag flags, cross-checked against justification and missing activities.
questions.answer_full: The audit counts lags and leads and flags negatives — leads are the red one; they let a successor start before its driver and quietly compress the path. Good news on this file: the delay reads as genuine, no lag manipulation detected, so nobody has inflated lags to absorb slip. Still, any long lag on the jetty path deserves a justification note — a lag is often a hidden activity (cure time, delivery) that should be a real, resourced bar. Cross-check the big ones against missing scope.

questions.q: Which activities run longer than 44 working days that I should break down?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: High-duration activities that hurt progress granularity.
questions.answer_full: The Health Review lists every activity over the 44-day DCMA limit. Long bars kill progress granularity — you can't see a 90-day activity slipping until it's too late, and they distort earned value. On a marine job the usual culprits are bulk pile-driving or a long silo slipform run. Break the offenders into monthly or milestone-based chunks so the update actually shows movement. Read the exact list off the report and prioritise any long bar sitting on the jetty (TF -18) or silo (TF -9) path.

questions.q: Do I have any circular logic or loops in the network?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Detects loops that stop the schedule calculating — a blocking gate before other metrics are trusted.
questions.answer_full: This is a blocking gate — a loop stops the network calculating, so no float, no critical path, no reliable finish until it's cleared. The Health Review scans for loops first. The fact we're getting a coherent +47-day forecast and a clean TF -18 on the jetty tells me the schedule is calculating cleanly, i.e. no open loops. If the check ever flags one, fix it before you read any other metric — everything downstream is meaningless until the network resolves.

questions.q: Do I have out-of-sequence progress, why did it happen, and can you fix it and hand me a corrected schedule?
questions.grounds: Schedule Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Flags OOS with a per-item cause, applies corrections, re-validates on the same engine, outputs a corrected XER/XML.
questions.answer_full: Yes — 12 activities progressed out of their planned logic. Usual causes: work started before its predecessor formally finished (access came early), or logic that no longer matches how crews are actually building. The Schedule Audit gives a per-item cause, lets you apply or edit a correction, re-validates on the same engine, then writes a corrected XER/XML to reimport. Twelve is manageable — but check none sit on the jetty path, because OOS there can flatter true progress and mask the slip we're reporting.

questions.q: Are my key milestones properly tied into logic on both sides, or are any dangling or detached?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review, Schedule Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Confirms milestones and activities are network-driven, not floating free.
questions.answer_full: The audit confirms each milestone has logic on both sides — a predecessor driving it and, for interim ones, a successor carrying it forward. A detached milestone floats free and reports a date nobody's schedule actually controls, which is dangerous for sectional-completion dates carrying LD exposure. With 3 open ends on the file, check none of them is a key milestone. Every contractual milestone — especially the jetty and silo handover dates — must be network-driven so its forecast moves honestly when work slips.

questions.q: Of all my logic problems, which affect completion versus cosmetic — give me a prioritized punch list to fix before resubmit.
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review, Schedule Audit, Constructability Review
questions.answer_sketch: Ranked to-do list separating completion-driving defects from housekeeping.
questions.answer_full: Priority order for resubmit: first, anything on the driving path — reconcile the out-of-sequence items and close any open end sitting on the jetty (TF -18) or silo (TF -9) chains, because those actually move the finish. Second, tidy the remaining open ends and any hard constraint suppressing float. Cosmetic last: long-duration breakdowns and relationship-type cleanup. In short, the completion-driving fixes are a handful; the rest is housekeeping for the consultant. Don't burn a week polishing cosmetics while the real recovery work waits.

questions.q: If I clean up these issues, will my finish date actually change?
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Estimates the completion effect of the fixes via the F9 keystone before rework.
questions.answer_full: Mostly no — and that's the message. Closing the 3 open ends and reconciling the 12 out-of-sequence items cleans the logic but won't pull the finish in; the +47-day slip is real, driven by physical jetty progress, not data defects. Run it through the what-if/F9 keystone to confirm before you rework. Don't let anyone hope the cleanup recovers time — real recovery comes from the levers we tested: jetty night shift ~+6 wd and a second piling crew ~+4 wd, both P6-verified.

questions.q: Do I have redundant or duplicate relationships cluttering the logic?
questions.grounds: GAP — not in the DCMA set or current audits
questions.answer_sketch: Not groundable yet: redundant-relationship detection isn't implemented.
questions.answer_full: Honest answer: the tool can't ground this yet. Redundant-relationship detection — links that add nothing because a longer logic path already governs — isn't in the DCMA set or the current audits, so I won't put a number on it. It's genuine clutter worth clearing, since it obscures the true driving path, but for now you'd spot it manually in P6 or a scheduling add-in. To ground it here we'd need a transitive-redundancy pass added to the logic audit. Everything else in this review stands.

catalog.blurb: What changed between schedule versions — revision to revision and update to update — and whether it's honest re-planning or a disguised slip.

questions.q: What actually changed between the approved baseline and the new revision — the headline before I read the whole thing?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Exec summary of every change category and severity.
questions.answer_full: Run the Baseline Revision Comparison exec summary first — it buckets every change (scope, durations, logic, calendar, constraints, milestones, WBS) with a severity flag before you wade into detail. On this job the headline is a finish moving out to ~20 Apr 2027 against the 9 Feb 2027 approved baseline, +47 working days, and the comparison reads it as genuine slip — no baseline logic or lag manipulation detected. Read the driver bridge next; ignore the cosmetic churn.

questions.q: The finish slipped in the revised baseline — break down what pushed it: added scope, longer durations, logic, or calendar?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Finish-slip driver bridge attributing the move to each change type.
questions.answer_full: The finish-slip driver bridge splits that +47 wd move across added scope, duration growth, logic edits and calendar changes. On this schedule it lands almost entirely on Marine & Jetty Works execution — pile driving to deck to fender, ~18 wd behind with total float -18 on the governing path — not on new scope or stretched durations. Engineering and procurement are broadly on track, so this reads as real site slippage the re-plan must recover, not a paper change.

questions.q: Which activities got added — real new scope or just re-decomposition — and which were deleted, and were any critical?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Added/removed activity lists flagged for scope growth and criticality.
questions.answer_full: Use the added/removed lists, but don't treat every addition as new scope — the tool flags whether an add is genuine scope or just re-decomposition (one activity split into several) and whether any added or deleted activity sits on the driving path. That's what matters: a deleted critical activity or added critical scope moves your claim indicators. Reconcile the flags against your change register before you accept the counts, and check nothing landed on the jetty chain unnoticed.

questions.q: Did total scope grow — activities, man-hours, budget — between the two baselines?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Quantifies scope growth to size potential scope creep for a change claim.
questions.answer_full: The comparison sizes scope growth three ways — activity count, man-hours (these are man-hours, not headcount) and loaded budget. That's your first measure of possible scope creep. If activities and man-hours jumped with no change order behind them, that's a change-claim indicator worth pursuing — the tool sizes it, it never establishes entitlement. Cross-check any budget growth against the cost-loading; percentage-only scope won't move the money line, so keep that figure qualitative unless the loading backs it.

questions.q: Show me every logic change — relationships added, removed, retyped — and which sit on the driving path.
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Logic-change diff filtered to path impact.
questions.answer_full: Pull the logic-change diff — relationships added, removed and retyped — then filter to the driving path, which is the only cut that matters. Edits off the critical chain are housekeeping. Here the governing path runs through the jetty (piling to deck to fender), so any relationship changes there get scrutiny. The comparison found no baseline logic or lag manipulation, so treat the edits as genuine re-planning unless the driver bridge says a specific change moved the finish.

questions.q: Which durations changed, and were any critical-path durations shortened without a stated reason?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Duration-change register flagging critical-path shortenings, a classic manipulation signal.
questions.answer_full: The duration-change register lists every stretched or shortened activity and specifically flags critical-path durations that were cut. A shortened critical duration with no stated reason is the classic manipulation tell — that's where you look hardest. On this schedule the analysis found no such gaming; the slip reads genuine. So if critical durations did move, get the planner's productivity or method justification. Absent one, treat a quiet critical-path cut as a red flag to raise with the consultant.

questions.q: Did anyone re-sequence work, add new constraints, or inflate the calendar to pull the finish in on paper?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Schedule Health Review, Calendar Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Sequence-reversal, added-constraint and calendar-change detection.
questions.answer_full: That's a three-part manipulation check — sequence reversals, newly added constraints, and calendar inflation (extra working days or shifts pulling the finish in on paper) — and you run all three. Here the tool found the delay genuine: no hidden constraint holding the date, no calendar padding. It did flag 12 out-of-sequence activities and 3 open ends to clean up. Fix those before resubmission so no one can argue the finish is an artefact rather than real driving logic.

questions.q: Did the critical path re-route to a different chain, and where did float migrate between the two baselines?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Criticality changes plus float-migration view showing who lost or gained slack.
questions.answer_full: Use the criticality-change and float-migration views together — they show whether the driving chain jumped work fronts and who lost or gained slack between the two baselines. On this project the jetty governs at total float -18, with the Silo Structure the near-critical second front at TF -9; that silo turns critical the moment the jetty slips further. So the migration view is telling you to manage two fronts, not one — plan any recovery against both or you'll just shift the bottleneck sideways.

questions.q: Which changes are material versus cosmetic, and did any activity keep the same work but get a new ID or name?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Material-vs-minor classification plus id/rename reconciliation for traceability.
questions.answer_full: The comparison classifies every change material versus minor and reconciles activities that kept the same work but got a new ID or name — so a rename doesn't surface as a false delete-plus-add. That reconciliation is what keeps the change count honest and traceable. Focus your review and the client conversation on the material set; the cosmetic churn — renames, code tidy-ups, re-decomposition — is noise you note but don't argue over. It stops you chasing changes that carry no schedule effect.

questions.q: Which contract milestones moved and by how many days — and are any 'renamed' ones actually the same milestone?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Milestone change table in working days, with similar-name reconciliation to avoid false remove+add.
questions.answer_full: The milestone change table gives each milestone's move in working days, with similar-name reconciliation so a renamed milestone isn't reported as one removed and another added. This is your sectional-completion exposure — every interim date that slipped carries its own LD risk, not just final handover. One caveat: the tool reads P6 milestone constraint dates, not the contract dates themselves, so reconcile each move against the actual contractual obligation before you report exposure to the client.

questions.q: Was the WBS restructured — branches added/removed or activities shuffled between nodes?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Structure diff revealing reorganisation that can hide scope.
questions.answer_full: The structure diff shows branches added or removed and activities shuffled between WBS nodes. Watch this one closely — reorganising the WBS is a common way to bury added scope or make a comparison hard to follow. If activities moved nodes, confirm total scope still reconciles: tie it back to the activity-added/removed and man-hour counts so nothing was quietly slipped in under a new branch. A clean re-plan keeps the WBS stable or explains every structural move it makes.

questions.q: Give me a manipulation check — anything that looks like gaming rather than genuine re-planning — and did DCMA quality get worse?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Rolls up suspicious signals as evidence (never a verdict) plus the DCMA quality delta.
questions.answer_full: The tool rolls up every suspicious signal — quiet critical-path duration cuts, added constraints, calendar padding, sequence reversals — as evidence, never a verdict; the judgement stays yours. It also gives the DCMA quality delta between versions. On this job those signals came back clean: the delay is genuine, no manipulation detected. DCMA-wise you still carry 12 out-of-sequence activities and 3 open ends to close. Present the evidence to the consultant as indicators, not accusations — let the data speak.

questions.q: Bottom line — is this revision a genuine recovery re-plan, or a slip dressed up to look better?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Exec summary and driver bridge together answer whether the finish improved through real logic.
questions.answer_full: Read the exec summary and driver bridge together and the answer is: genuine. The finish moved to ~20 Apr 2027, +47 wd, and the analysis found no logic, lag, constraint or calendar manipulation behind it — this is real execution loss at the jetty, SPI 0.66, 40.4% actual against 61.4% planned. Hold that honest position; don't dress it up. Your credible recovery case is the jetty night shift (~+6 wd) plus a second piling crew (~+4 wd), both P6-verified — that's the real re-plan.

questions.q: The contractor's update shows a delay — is it real by P6 F9, and which logic or lag changes did they slip in that aren't in the baseline?
questions.grounds: Consultant Review, Update vs Update
questions.answer_sketch: Before/after but-for verification plus the driving logic/lag change table.
questions.answer_full: Run Consultant Review's before/after but-for: strip the contractor's logic and lag changes, re-run through the P6 F9 keystone, and see what delay actually survives. That separates real slip from anything engineered into the update. Here the honest read is the delay is genuine — F9 confirms ~+47 wd — with no lag or logic manipulation detected. Present any change table as indicators for the claims discussion; the tool shows cause and concurrency, it never says entitled — that's a contractual determination.

questions.q: Between last month's update and this one, what changed on the driving path and did the contractor overstate progress?
questions.grounds: Update vs Update, Update Analysis, EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Period progress and critical-path timeline cross-checked against reported EV/Performance%.
questions.answer_full: Update vs Update gives you the period delta on the driving path plus reported progress, and you cross-check earned value against it. Overall the job sits at 40.4% actual against 61.4% planned — about 21 points behind, SPI 0.66 — so there's no room for optimistic claiming. If reported EV outran what the critical-path activities physically achieved this window, that's your overstatement flag; watch the jetty front hardest. Also review the 12 out-of-sequence activities, which can make period progress read better than it truly is.

questions.q: Was each baseline change approved through a change order, who made it and when, and does the revision still comply with the schedule spec?
questions.grounds: GAP — no change-order link, edit attribution, or contract-spec model
questions.answer_sketch: Not groundable: the tool compares end-states, not authorisation, authorship or spec compliance.
questions.answer_full: Honest answer: the tool can't ground this. It compares end-states — what changed between two schedules — not whether each change was authorised, who made it, when, or whether the revision meets your schedule specification. To answer it I'd need a change-order/approval link per change, per-edit author-and-timestamp audit data (which P6 exports don't reliably carry), and a model of the client's spec to test against. For now, run the comparison and reconcile each material change against your change register by hand.

catalog.blurb: The money picture — earned vs planned vs spent, variances, curves, and where cost and performance forecasting still falls short.

questions.q: How much value have I earned versus what I planned to earn by this data date?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: EV vs PV gap showing whether we are delivering the planned value.
questions.answer_full: By the 19 Jul data date you've earned about two-thirds of the value you planned to — SPI 0.66. In progress terms that's 40.4% actually earned against 61.4% planned, a 21-point hole. That gap isn't spread evenly: engineering and procurement are broadly on plan, so nearly all the missing value sits in the Marine & Jetty works. Treat the shortfall as a jetty-execution problem, not a whole-project one.

questions.q: What's my schedule variance and cost variance in dollars?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: variance (EV−PV) and CV (EV−AC) in $ for the client report.
questions.answer_full: Both variances are negative. Schedule variance (EV−PV) is the big one — at SPI 0.66 you've under-earned by roughly a third of this period's planned value, driven almost entirely by the jetty. Cost variance (EV−AC) is milder: CPI 0.94 says you're spending about 6% more than you're earning. The dashboard and Excel export carry the exact dollar figures per discipline; the story is a schedule problem first, a modest cost-efficiency problem second.

questions.q: How much have I spent to date versus plan, and is my percent-spent running ahead of percent-complete?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: AC vs PV plus AC/BAC vs actual% as an early-overspend warning.
questions.answer_full: Yes, but only slightly. CPI 0.94 means for every unit of value earned you've spent about 1.06 — so percent-spent is running a few points ahead of your 40.4% complete, call it low-40s percent spent against 40.4% earned. That's a mild burn-rate warning, not a blow-out, and because the schedule is genuinely cost-loaded the number is real. Watch it monthly; if CPI keeps sliding as the jetty drags on, that gap widens.

questions.q: Which disciplines are over or under budget, and how's the budget split across engineering, procurement and construction?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Per-category BAC vs AC ranking and the BAC weight distribution.
questions.answer_full: Pull the per-category BAC-vs-AC view — it ranks every discipline over or under. The shape to expect on a bulk terminal: construction (marine/jetty, silo, civils) carries the lion's share of BAC, with engineering and procurement a thinner slice. Engineering and procurement are tracking to plan, so the cost pressure sits in construction — specifically the jetty, where slow progress is pulling CPI down to 0.94. That's where I'd focus the cost review, not across the board.

questions.q: Am I over-claiming — where is earned value higher than the cost I've actually spent, by discipline?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Per-category EV vs AC flags optimistic progress claims versus real spend.
questions.answer_full: Overall you're the opposite — CPI 0.94 means spend is slightly ahead of earned, so no global over-claim. But check it discipline by discipline in the per-category EV-vs-AC view: any front showing EV well above AC is claiming progress it hasn't paid for. I'd scrutinise the jetty especially — with 12 out-of-sequence activities in the file, some earned value there may be booked against work started ahead of its predecessors. Reconcile those claims against physical installation before you report them.

questions.q: Is my schedule even cost-loaded, or are these percent-only numbers — and which scope has no budget loaded?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Tells whether CPI is real; lists zero-BAC scope excluded from the $ figures.
questions.answer_full: This one is genuinely cost-loaded, so CPI 0.94 is a real spend-efficiency figure, not a percent-only proxy — you can trust the money read. Do check the category view for any zero-BAC scope: milestones, level-of-effort and late-added activities often carry no budget and silently drop out of the EV/AC totals. If a big construction package shows zero BAC, your CPI is being computed on a partial base — flag and load it before the next client report.

questions.q: Is Planned Value coming straight from P6 or are you re-deriving it?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: P6 omits Schedule%/PV, so the planned side is re-derived — sets confidence on the $ figures.
questions.answer_full: Re-deriving it. P6's XML doesn't export a Schedule% or a Planned Value curve, so the tool rebuilds the planned side from the baseline dates and the loaded budget — a sound approximation, not a number lifted straight from P6. Actual cost and earned value come from the loaded costs directly. So treat SPI 0.66 as directional; for the hard schedule position lean on the P6 F9 delay of +47 working days, which is computed, not re-derived.

questions.q: Show me the spend S-curve — planned vs actual cumulative cost — and am I burning faster than planned?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, EVM, Consultant Review
questions.answer_sketch: Cumulative cost S-curve with slope showing whether cash outruns value.
questions.answer_full: The curve will show actual cumulative cost sitting below the planned line — but don't read that as underspending. You're below plan because you're 21 points behind on work, not because you're saving money. The honest read is cost-per-unit-of-progress: CPI 0.94 says each bit of work is costing about 6% more than budgeted. So you're burning slower in total but less efficiently per unit. As the jetty recovers, expect actual cost to climb steeply back toward the plan.

questions.q: Which work fronts are burning budget but not showing progress?
questions.grounds: EVM, Update Analysis
questions.answer_sketch: AC rising with flat actual% flags trouble activities before they blow the budget.
questions.answer_full: Cross the per-category AC-vs-actual% view with the Update Analysis overdue list — any front where cost is climbing but percent-complete is flat is the one to grab. On this job that's the Marine & Jetty works: 18 working days behind, dragging CPI, and sitting on the governing path. Pile-driving in particular soaks up plant and crew hours against slow physical output. Watch the silo structure too — 9 days behind and next in line to turn critical.

questions.q: Build me a one-page cost/EVM dashboard for the client and export the numbers to Excel.
questions.grounds: Reporting Studio, EVM
questions.answer_sketch: SPI/CPI/variance/curve composed into a PDF/Word plus an Excel export per category.
questions.answer_full: Reporting Studio does this in one pass. Compose the one-pager with the KPI tiles (SPI 0.66, CPI 0.94, 40.4% vs 61.4%, +47 wd), the planned-vs-actual S-curve and the per-discipline BAC/AC table, then export the same content to Excel — one row per category so the client's cost team can pivot it. Lead the page with a single line: 21 points behind, driven by the jetty, cost efficiency broadly holding. Keep the numbers straight off this snapshot.

questions.q: Is my CPI trending better or worse over the last few updates?
questions.grounds: Power BI live dashboards
questions.answer_sketch: Snapshots store CPI per import; a CPI-trend view arrives with the live dashboards.
questions.answer_full: Right now I can give you today's CPI — 0.94 — but not the trend line yet. Every import already stores CPI in the snapshot history, so the data is there; the CPI-over-time view is landing with the Power BI live dashboards, still in build. In the meantime, open the last two or three snapshots and read the CPI off each by hand — if it's sliding from near 1.0 toward 0.94 as the jetty drags, that's your early cost-efficiency erosion and worth calling out now.

questions.q: At this CPI, what will the whole job cost at completion, how much more will I spend, and what CPI do I need to still land on budget?
questions.grounds: GAP — EVM has CPI but no EAC/ETC/TCPI tiles
questions.answer_sketch: Not surfaced: EAC=BAC/CPI, ETC and TCPI would follow from CPI/EV/BAC once a forecast module exists.
questions.answer_full: Honestly, the tool can't ground EAC, ETC or TCPI yet — it computes CPI but carries no cost-forecasting module. The mechanics are simple once it does: EAC ≈ BAC ÷ CPI, so at 0.94 you'd be looking at roughly a 6% overrun if today's efficiency holds; ETC is EAC minus what you've spent; TCPI is the efficiency you'd need on the remaining work to still hit BAC. I can walk you through those by hand from your BAC, but I won't quote a figure the tool hasn't produced.

questions.q: What's the cost of my current delay — how much prolongation am I carrying, and what's my month-by-month forward cashflow?
questions.grounds: GAP — delay_days and baseline S-curve are ingredients only
questions.answer_sketch: Not computed: monetary prolongation and forward monthly cash forecast aren't produced yet.
questions.answer_full: The tool can't put a money figure on the delay yet. It gives you the delay in hard terms — +47 working days by P6 F9 — and the baseline cost curve, but it doesn't multiply your daily prolongation/extended-preliminaries rate across those days or roll a forward month-by-month cashflow. To ground it I'd need your time-related preliminaries rate per day; prolongation is then roughly that rate times the 47 days. Keep this as an indicator of exposure, not a claimed sum — and note it feeds the EOT work still in build.

questions.q: My cost-based SPI will drift back toward 1.0 as I near completion even while running late — give me a time-based / earned-schedule read of schedule performance instead.
questions.grounds: GAP — delay-in-working-days is the partial time-based counterpart; a formal earned-schedule SPI(t) index/trend is not produced
questions.answer_sketch: Not produced: the tool gives cost-based SPI (a known-unreliable late-stage indicator) and delay in working days, not an earned-schedule SPI(t) index or its trend.
questions.answer_full: You're right, and it's the correct instinct — cost-based SPI always creeps back to 1.0 near the end even on a late job, so 0.66 will flatter you later. A true earned-schedule SPI(t) index and trend isn't produced yet; that's a known gap. What the tool gives as the time-based counterpart is the P6 F9 delay itself — +47 working days, forecast finish ~20 Apr 2027 against a 9 Feb baseline. Report off that number, not off SPI, as you move into the back end of the job.

catalog.blurb: Whether the plan can be manned, what productivity it assumes, and whether the labour curve is real.

questions.q: What's my peak manpower, when does it hit, and does it line up with my key milestones?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Productivity & Resource Intelligence, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Labour peak, its timing, and whether it coincides with the critical work.
questions.answer_full: Read it off the man-hour histogram — and remember these are man-hours, not heads, so converting to a crew count needs a crew-size assumption. Your peak should sit over the marine/jetty and silo window, where the governing path (pile-driving to deck to fender, TF -18) lives. My worry is timing: we're 21 points behind and adding a night shift plus a second piling crew, so the peak sharpens and moves right just as the silo (TF -9) loads. Confirm it still lands before your key milestones, not after.

questions.q: Is my manpower histogram realistic, or does it spike unrealistically week to week?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Flags unrealistic spikes and troughs in the labour curve.
questions.answer_full: Look for saw-tooth week-to-week jumps — that's the tell of an unstaffable curve. Expect the recovery levers you're testing (jetty night shift, second piling crew) to add real spikes, so don't confuse a genuine push with an artefact. Where engineering and procurement are on track and carry float, smooth by shifting effort off them rather than ramping bodies. A curve that doubles man-hours in a week won't get manned — flatten it before you commit to it.

questions.q: Is this schedule resource-loaded at all, or just a logic network — and how many man-hours does it assume by discipline?
questions.grounds: Productivity & Resource Intelligence, EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Establishes whether any resource analysis is possible and gives the man-hour split.
questions.answer_full: Yes — it carries man-hours by discipline, which is how we're giving you any manpower read at all; it's also cost-loaded, so CPI 0.94 is real money, not percent-only. Confirm those are genuine P6 resource assignments and not just cost dressed up as labour. The bulk sits in Marine & Jetty and Silo Structure. One caveat: the tool reads P6-form resources read-only — if a package was never loaded, it shows zero, not a guess.

questions.q: Given the concrete and rebar quantities, are these durations achievable at normal crew productivity — flag the over-optimistic ones?
questions.grounds: Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Checks implied output against the norm KB and lists activities exceeding it.
questions.answer_full: Run Productivity & Resource Intelligence — it back-calculates the implied daily output behind each duration and flags any that beat the 151-item norm KB. On this job I'd scrutinise the silo concrete/slipform and the jetty deck pours first. One honest limit: it needs the quantities loaded on the activities — where P6 carries no quantity it can't check that line and won't invent one. If pile-driving is already 18 wd behind, its baseline rate was likely optimistic to start with.

questions.q: Can this plan be manned — is the peak and ramp-up feasible, and does it demobilize sensibly or fall off a cliff?
questions.grounds: Productivity & Resource Intelligence, Baseline Revision Comparison
questions.answer_sketch: Judges peak, week-on-week ramp and end-taper against realistic recruitment/mobilization.
questions.answer_full: Judge it against real recruitment, not a smooth curve. The ramp shouldn't need labour doubling week-on-week, and your recovery adds a night shift and a second piling crew — marine-specialist trades you can't just conjure, so confirm they're sourceable before you bank the +6 and +4 wd. Watch the tail too: it should taper into commissioning, not fall off a cliff and leave punch/handover under-manned. A peak you can't man is a paper peak.

questions.q: Is my finish limited by logic or by manpower — is any of the delay resource-driven?
questions.grounds: Productivity & Resource Intelligence, What-if / scenario engine, Update Analysis
questions.answer_sketch: Distinguishes a logic-limited finish from a resource-limited one, since the fix differs.
questions.answer_full: Partly resource-driven — and that matters, because the fix differs. The jetty slip is a site-execution problem on the governing path: pile-driving output below plan, not a logic error (no baseline logic/lag manipulation, only 12 out-of-sequence). The tell is that adding capacity moves F9 — second piling crew +4 wd, night shift +6 wd, both P6-verified. If it were purely logic-limited, extra crews wouldn't shift the date. So production at the jetty is limiting the finish, not the network.

questions.q: We're behind on SPI — is it a manpower shortfall or a sequencing problem, and which discipline is worst?
questions.grounds: EVM, Update Analysis, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Attributes the slip to under-manning versus bad sequencing and names the worst trade.
questions.answer_full: It's production, not sequencing. SPI 0.66 is being dragged by the marine/jetty front — pile-driving is running below planned output — while engineering and procurement are broadly on track. Sequencing is basically sound: only 12 out-of-sequence and no baseline manipulation detected. Worst discipline is Marine & Jetty Works, ~18 wd behind on the governing path (TF -18), with Silo Structure second at ~9 wd (TF -9). So the pressure this week is manpower/productivity at the jetty, not re-logic.

questions.q: How many concurrent work-fronts does the driving path assume — can I man them all at once?
questions.grounds: Update Analysis, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Checks whether the driving path spreads labour across more fronts than can be crewed.
questions.answer_full: The governing path today is the jetty chain — pile-driving to deck to fender — which is largely one front at a time, so it isn't over-spread at source. The risk is your recovery: a night shift plus a second piling crew means two piling operations running while the silo (TF -9) also loads. Check you can crew specialist marine trades across all of them at once. The tool shows concurrent activities per period; the man-hour peak tests whether the aggregate is staffable.

questions.q: What productivity rates did the planner assume behind these durations, and are they credible?
questions.grounds: Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Surfaces the norm assumptions underpinning durations so they can be challenged.
questions.answer_full: Productivity & Resource Intelligence surfaces exactly that — it back-derives the output rate implied by each duration and shows it against the norm KB with its source, so you can challenge the planner's assumption rather than argue blind. The one to interrogate here is the pile-driving rate: if the baseline assumed an output we're now missing by 18 working days, either that norm was optimistic or the marine conditions are harder than planned. It shows provenance and won't fabricate a rate for you.

questions.q: Did resource loading change between revisions — and did the new revision flatten the manpower peak or just postpone it?
questions.grounds: Baseline Revision Comparison, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Shows added/removed/changed assignments and whether resequencing genuinely relieved the peak.
questions.answer_full: Baseline Revision Comparison plus the resource layer shows it — added, removed and changed assignments between the two revisions, and whether the man-hour peak genuinely dropped or just slid to the right. The tell: if total man-hours are unchanged but the peak moved later, they postponed the problem, they didn't relieve it — a slip dressed as a re-plan. Read it alongside the finish-slip driver bridge so you can see whether the resequence actually bought time or only reprofiled the labour.

questions.q: For the remaining quantities, how many crews and how long will it really take — can that beat the plan?
questions.grounds: Duration & Resource Calculation, Productivity & Resource Intelligence, What-if / scenario engine
questions.answer_sketch: Bottom-up remaining-work duration from quantities (Duration & Resource Calculation, in progress).
questions.answer_full: Honest answer: the true bottom-up — remaining quantities to crews to duration — is the Duration & Resource Calculation module, and that's still in build, so I won't hand you a hard crew count off it yet. Today I can approximate it with the what-if engine and the productivity norms as a sense-check against the plan, but treat that as an estimate. Once the calc lands you'll get quantity-driven crew and duration figures you can set against the remaining plan properly.

questions.q: Are any resources over-allocated, and if I level to a realistic crew cap, how much does the finish slip?
questions.grounds: GAP — what-if adds crews but does not detect conflicts or level to a limit
questions.answer_sketch: Not groundable: over-allocation detection and automatic resource leveling aren't implemented.
questions.answer_full: The tool can't ground this one yet. The what-if engine adds crews and reruns F9, but it doesn't detect over-allocation conflicts or level to a crew cap, so I can't give you an honest leveled finish date. To answer it properly we'd need over-allocation detection plus automatic leveling to a resource limit — not built. For now, level in P6 against your real crew caps and re-import, and I'll read the slip that comes out; I won't invent a number.

catalog.blurb: Managing by package and handoff — who's behind, whether interface milestones are tied down on both sides, and where trades collide.

questions.q: Rank my subcontractors / scope packages by how far behind each is against plan — who needs the pressure this week?
questions.grounds: Update Analysis, EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Worst-performer ranking by package/WBS from planned-vs-actual by activity code, to direct where to push — a PM manages by package, not just by engineering/procurement/construction discipline.
questions.answer_full: Manage this one by package, not just by engineering/procurement/construction. Rank each sub's activities planned-vs-actual by activity code and WBS. On this job the answer's clear: the marine/jetty package is your worst performer — about 18 wd behind, float -18, sitting on the governing path, so that's where the pressure goes this week. Silo Structure is second, ~9 wd behind (TF -9) and about to turn critical. Engineering and procurement are broadly on plan. Overall SPI 0.66, 40.4% actual vs 61.4% planned. Push the jetty sub first, silo second.

questions.q: Which activities are interface handoffs between subcontractors, or between me and the client (free-issue, access handover, permits), and are those interface milestones tied into logic on both sides?
questions.grounds: Schedule Health Review, Schedule Audit, Constructability Review + Construction Knowledge Base
questions.answer_sketch: Confirms interface milestones are network-driven on both sides; a dangling or one-sided interface point hides the highest-risk, most-claimed handoffs and defeats accountability.
questions.answer_full: Pull the interface points out and check each is network-driven on both sides — a real driving predecessor feeding it and a driven successor coming off it. The Audit already flags 3 open ends and 12 out-of-sequence items; any of those sitting on an access handover, free-issue or permit milestone is a one-sided interface, and that's exactly where accountability and claims exposure hide. Tie them down both ends. The jetty handoff chain (pile-driving to deck to fender) is the one to protect first, then let Constructability/KB confirm the sequence is buildable.

questions.q: Are too many trades stacked in the same work area at the same time on the driving path — is the plan spatially congested and unbuildable?
questions.grounds: GAP — schedule has no area-by-time occupancy model; trade-stacking / spatial congestion not computed
questions.answer_sketch: Not groundable: the tool reads logic and dates, not spatial occupancy by area over time (a leading cause of real productivity loss and interface clashes).
questions.answer_full: Honestly, the tool can't ground this one yet — it reads logic and dates, not who occupies which area when, so I can't compute trade-stacking or spatial congestion for you. To answer it properly it would need a zone/area code on each activity and an area-by-time occupancy model run over the driving path. For now judge it by eye: on this job the jetty deck, between piling finishing and fender install starting, is the obvious pinch-point. Walk it with the sub and confirm the deck can actually carry the crews the plan assumes working there at once.

catalog.blurb: The final phase where jobs quietly overrun — testing, commissioning, punch-list, handover and close-out scope and timing.

questions.q: How is commissioning and testing tracking against plan, and are the systems-completion / T&C activities now on the critical path to handover?
questions.grounds: EVM, Critical Path Analyzer, Update Analysis
questions.answer_sketch: Isolates the commissioning/T&C phase's progress and tests whether the T&C tail — not construction — is driving the handover date; a poor overall SPI is often the commissioning tail.
questions.answer_full: Right now the handover date isn't being driven by commissioning — it's the Marine & Jetty works (pile-driving to deck to fenders, TF -18 wd) sitting on the governing path. But don't relax: the whole T&C tail hangs off that chain, so every day the jetty loses pushes commissioning start right into the handover milestone. Isolate the commissioning category in EVM and track it as its own front now. Overall SPI 0.66 is a jetty story today, but as construction closes out that tail becomes what governs — get ahead of it.

questions.q: Does my schedule actually contain the commissioning, testing, pre-comm, punch-list and handover activities it needs for this project type, or does it jump from construction straight to completion?
questions.grounds: Constructability Review + Construction Knowledge Base, Schedule Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Checks the T&C/handover chain against the project-type playbook and flags absent commissioning activities (execution scope, within the construction/execution missing-activity remit).
questions.answer_full: Run Constructability against the marine-terminal playbook before you trust the tail. For a grain terminal I'd expect energisation, loop checks, conveyor no-load then loaded runs, ship-loader commissioning, a throughput/performance trial, punch-listing, then handover — not construction straight into completion. The KB missing-activity check is execution-scoped, so it will flag any of those that are absent. If the schedule jumps from 'jetty complete' to a handover milestone, that scope is living in someone's head, not in the logic. Add it and re-plan the tail properly.

questions.q: Is there enough time between mechanical completion and the handover milestone for testing and commissioning, or has the commissioning tail been compressed to hold the date on paper?
questions.grounds: Critical Path Analyzer, Calendar Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Measures the working-time window between mechanical completion and handover to expose a squeezed T&C period — a classic reason handover slips even when construction finishes on time.
questions.answer_full: That's exactly where terminals bleed. Measure the working-days window between mechanical completion and the handover milestone in the Critical Path Analyzer, then read it against the marine/coastal calendar in Calendar Audit — weather eats into any commissioning window on this coast. With the jetty ~18 wd behind and the finish already +47 wd out, the classic move is to crush the T&C tail to hold the date on paper. If the handover milestone hasn't moved but MC has, commissioning has been compressed — protect that window, don't borrow from it.

questions.q: Are my close-out activities — as-builts, O&M manuals, final documentation, demobilisation, retention release — in the schedule and tied into logic, or left floating at the end?
questions.grounds: Schedule Audit, Schedule Health Review, Constructability Review + Construction Knowledge Base
questions.answer_sketch: Open-end/dangling detection plus the KB sequence catch close-out scope that's omitted or left unsequenced, which otherwise delays final account, retention and demob.
questions.answer_full: Check this now — close-out is where your 3 open ends almost certainly live. Run the Schedule Audit open-end/dangling check and the Health Review: as-builts, O&M manuals, final documentation, demob and retention release get routinely left floating at the end with no driving logic. If they're unsequenced or missing they won't calculate through, and final account and retention release will slip well past handover even after the jetty catches up. Tie each into logic on both sides and put them behind the handover milestone, not beside it.

catalog.blurb: Design deliverables and long-lead items — progress, criticality, handoffs and delivery risk.

questions.q: How's engineering doing against baseline — isolate the design category's SPI and % complete, separate from construction?
questions.grounds: EVM, Update Analysis
questions.answer_sketch: Design-discipline SPI and Schedule%/Performance% so a poor overall SPI isn't misattributed.
questions.answer_full: Split it out — don't let the design office wear the field's delay. Overall the job is SPI 0.66, 40.4% actual vs 61.4% planned, but that ~21-point deficit lives in Marine & Jetty Works (~18 wd behind, TF -18), not engineering. Filter EVM/Update Analysis to the design category and you'll see its own SPI and Schedule% sitting close to plan. Report engineering's number separately so the client reads the real story: the problem is site execution at the jetty, not the drawings.

questions.q: Which discipline is dragging my overall SPI down — upstream design/procurement or the field?
questions.grounds: EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Pinpoints whether the problem is upstream or in construction.
questions.answer_full: The field — specifically the marine works. Engineering and procurement are broadly on track here; the 0.66 overall SPI and the ~21-point gap (40.4% vs 61.4%) are driven by Marine & Jetty Works, ~18 wd behind and at TF -18 on the governing path, with Silo Structure second at ~9 wd (TF -9). Rank the per-category SPI in EVM and you'll see design and procurement near plan while construction carries the whole deficit. Point recovery at the jetty, not upstream.

questions.q: Show planned vs actual for every IFC drawing activity, and which engineering deliverables sit on the critical path.
questions.grounds: Update Analysis, EVM, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Late design packages by code and the deliverables that actually drive the finish.
questions.answer_full: Pull the design category in Update Analysis and lay planned vs actual against every IFC package by activity code, then cross that list with the Critical Path Analyzer driving path. On this job you'll find few or no engineering deliverables actually governing completion — the driving chain runs pile driving → deck → fender install at the jetty. So flag any late IFC package, but judge it by whether it feeds that marine front; drawings feeding high-float work aren't your problem this week.

questions.q: Is design late enough to threaten construction start, or still inside float?
questions.grounds: Critical Path Analyzer, Update Analysis, EVM
questions.answer_sketch: Whether late design is on the driving path to first construction or merely uncomfortable.
questions.answer_full: Test it against logic, not gut. Run the late design packages through the Critical Path Analyzer: if a package feeds the jetty chain (TF -18) any slip bites immediately; if it feeds work with float it's uncomfortable, not governing. On current reads engineering isn't on the driving path — the +47 wd finish slip is site execution at the marine works. So most late design is still inside float, but keep a close watch on anything feeding the jetty or the Silo Structure (TF -9).

questions.q: Which long-lead items are on the critical path, and rank them by how little float is left?
questions.grounds: Critical Path Analyzer, Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Long-lead chains controlling completion, prioritized for expediting by remaining float.
questions.answer_full: Filter to your procurement/delivery activities, tag the long-lead items, and sort by total float from the Critical Path Analyzer. Anything feeding the jetty chain (TF -18) or Silo Structure (TF -9) is already in the hole and expedites first; positive-float items can wait. The governing path here is pile driving → deck → fender install, so prioritise fenders and any piling/marine-plant deliveries. Confirm each long-lead item is logic-tied to its install, not floating on a date — Schedule Health flags 3 open ends worth checking.

questions.q: What's the required-on-site date for each long-lead item, and if a delivery slips 30 days what does it do to the finish?
questions.grounds: Critical Path Analyzer, What-if / scenario engine
questions.answer_sketch: Back-calculated ROS dates plus an F9-exact finish impact of a vendor slip.
questions.answer_full: Back-calculate each ROS date from its install start less rigging/prep in the Critical Path Analyzer, then model the 30-day slip in the what-if engine — the finish move comes out P6 F9-exact, not a guess. For an item feeding the jetty (TF -18) expect close to day-for-day pain on the +47 wd position; for a float-cushioned item the finish may not move until that float is eaten. Run each delivery individually so you know which are genuinely date-critical and which carry slack.

questions.q: If I air-freight the long-lead item and cut 20 days off delivery, does it pull my finish in?
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine
questions.answer_sketch: Tests whether expediting recovers the finish or just adds cost.
questions.answer_full: Only if that item is on the governing path — otherwise you're paying to create float you never use. Model the 20-day pull in the what-if engine (dates stay P6 F9-exact). If it feeds the jetty chain driving the +47 wd slip, you may claw days back; if it feeds Silo Structure (TF -9) or floated work, the finish holds and the airfreight premium buys nothing. Check it before you authorise the freight — the schedule will tell you whether it's worth the money.

questions.q: Are any installs scheduled before their material delivery finishes, and does every major item have a delivery activity feeding its installation?
questions.grounds: Schedule Audit, Update Analysis, Constructability Review
questions.answer_sketch: Catches install-before-delivery OOS and confirms the procure-deliver-install link per package.
questions.answer_full: Run the Schedule Audit for out-of-sequence and the Constructability check for the procure→deliver→install chain. The audit already flags 12 out-of-sequence activities — see whether any are installs statused ahead of their material delivery, which would be flattering your progress. Then confirm every major item (fenders, piling steel, silo steel, mechanical) has a delivery activity actually feeding its install, not an install hanging off a bare date. Any missing delivery link is a hidden risk and a candidate correction — the tool can hand you a corrected XER.

questions.q: Are procurement lead times modeled as real durations or hidden inside FS lags, and are delivery dates logic-driven or hard-constrained?
questions.grounds: Schedule Audit, Schedule Health Review
questions.answer_sketch: Exposes lead times buried as lags and constraints faking delivery dates.
questions.answer_full: Ask this before you trust the delivery dates. Run Schedule Audit for lags and Schedule Health for constraints. Lead time buried in a long FS lag is invisible work — it can't be progressed, resourced or expedited, and it hides slip, so pull it out as a real delivery activity. And if delivery dates are pinned by mandatory/finish constraints instead of PO→fabricate→ship logic, they show fake float and mask the true position. The delay reads genuine here, but clean the procurement logic so it stays that way.

questions.q: The delay's blamed on late vendor drawings — verify it against baseline vs update, and are there EOT indicators for late information?
questions.grounds: Consultant Review, Claims / TIA reference
questions.answer_sketch: Confirms or refutes that late deliverables drove the delay, with late-information EOT indicators.
questions.answer_full: Don't accept the blame line at face value — test it. Run Consultant Review (baseline-vs-update, but-for) to see whether late vendor drawings actually sit on the path that moved the finish. On this schedule the driver is the jetty marine works, not design, so a 'late drawings' narrative may not hold up. If the deliverables do drive it, the Claims/TIA reference surfaces late-information EOT indicators — indicators only, I won't call it an entitlement. Either way you get evidence, not opinion, to put to the client.

questions.q: Show completed engineering not yet flowing into procurement — where's the handoff stalling — and is the design-procure-fabricate-deliver-install sequence complete per the playbook?
questions.grounds: Update Analysis, Schedule Audit, Construction Knowledge Base
questions.answer_sketch: Stalled-handoff detection and each package's chain checked against the KB sequence.
questions.answer_full: Use Update Analysis to find design packages marked complete whose downstream procurement hasn't started — that's your stalled handoff. Then run each package's chain against the Construction Knowledge Base sequence (design → procure → fabricate → deliver → install) and flag any broken link; Schedule Audit's 3 open ends may be sitting right there. Engineering and procurement are broadly on track here, so expect few stalls — but any completed drawing not triggering its PO is float you're quietly burning, worth chasing before it ever reaches the jetty.

Missing activities make the path look shorter than reality, so this matters before you trust the +47 wd. Add the real steps and re-run F9 — the honest finish is usually worse, not better.

questions.q: If I re-sequence to start Area B before Area A finishes, is that even constructable?

questions.answer_sketch: Checks a recovery re-sequence against constructability rules before committing.

On the jetty the real constraint is single-berth working: you often can't run two piling fronts in one area without the rigs fouling. That's exactly why the 2nd-piling-crew what-if only returned ~+4 wd. Prove it's buildable before you commit it.

questions.q: Are there missing activities that, once added, would eat the recovery I think I have?

questions.answer_sketch: Avoids building a recovery plan on an incomplete schedule.

If the review finds missing jetty steps (cure times, fender pre-assembly, commissioning checks), adding them back can swallow part of that recovery before you even start. questions.q: Which delay analysis method fits my situation — TIA, windows, or as-planned vs as-built — given how progressed my data is?

questions.q: Is this delay excusable or on me — attribute the driving delay to employer/neutral versus contractor cause?

questions.q: Is this a money claim or just extra time — compensable versus excusable?

If you can evidence an employer act (late access, variations) it moves toward compensable; a neutral event like exceptional weather reads excusable-only (time, not money). Confirm compensability with your commercial and claims team — the schedule supports the time picture, not the money.

questions.q: How many working days of delay can I actually justify, and does the corrected but-for schedule back up that number?

But claim quantum is only the critical delay attributable to specific events, isolated in the corrected but-for run — not the whole 47, which mixes your own execution slip in. Run Consultant Review's but-for to strip out what's self-caused; whatever remains on the driving path is the number you can stand behind. Indicator only, never entitlement.

questions.q: The employer's drawings came late — did that push my critical path or just eat float?

questions.answer_sketch: Tests whether the employer event sat on the driving path or was absorbed by float.
questions.answer_full: Test it in the what-if engine — impact the drawing dates and re-run F9. On today's picture engineering is broadly on track and the driving path runs through jetty piling (TF -18), so unless those drawings feed the marine works directly, a late drawing likely sat on a floated chain and was absorbed rather than pushing completion. If it fed the jetty, it shows as movement at the finish. Only an event that moves the F9 finish carries a time impact — that's the indicator.

questions.q: Break my slip into weather, employer and me, and were the weather days worse than a competent contractor should have allowed for?
questions.grounds: Weather Impact, Consultant Review, Calendar Audit

questions.answer_full: On the schedule, the +47 wd concentrates on jetty execution (TF -18) with no employer event on the driving path, so the visible split is heavily contractor/execution. To carve out a weather share, run Weather Impact for this coastal/marine site: it compares actual adverse days against site-type norms, and only days beyond what a competent marine contractor should have allowed for read as potentially excusable. The employer share needs your causation record overlaid. This is an indicator split, not an agreed apportionment.

questions.q: Is there concurrent delay here — my delays running at the same time as the employer's — and was I pacing or genuinely behind?
questions.grounds: Consultant Review, Critical Path Analyzer, Claims / TIA reference

questions.answer_full: Concurrency needs two independent critical delays in the same window. Today only one chain is truly critical — the jetty at TF -18; the Silo Structure at TF -9 is near-critical, not yet co-critical, so on the schedule face there isn't genuine concurrency. Watch it: if the jetty slips further and the silo goes critical you could get overlapping delay. Pacing versus genuinely-behind is a causation judgement the schedule can't settle — flag it, but your claims consultant decides. Indicators only.

questions.q: Show me as-planned versus as-built on the critical path — where did I lose the time?

questions.answer_full: The tool overlays planned, earned and actual on the critical path — you'll see the baseline curve pulling to 61.4% by the data date while actual sits at 40.4%, the ~21-point gap opening from where the jetty piling started falling behind. That divergence point on the marine chain is where the time went. It's a strong exhibit for the client, but it's descriptive — it shows where and when slippage happened, not who caused it. Pair it with the causation record for the claim story.

questions.q: If the piling or the RFI answer slips N days, model the prospective time impact as a TIA fragnet.
questions.grounds: What-if / scenario engine, Critical Path Analyzer
questions.answer_sketch: Runs an impacted-as-planned fragnet through F9 for the net prospective impact.
questions.answer_full: Yes — build the fragnet in the what-if engine and run it through P6 F9. Insert the delay (a piling extension or the RFI hold) into the impacted-as-planned network and read the net movement at completion, on P6-exact dates — the same keystone that produced +47 wd today. Only the portion that moves the finish counts as impact; anything absorbed by float doesn't. Keep it as a prospective indicator exhibit for the claim, with quantum to be agreed by your consultant.

questions.q: How should I slice this into windows for a windows/time-slice analysis, and can I isolate the events or is it a global claim?

questions.answer_sketch: Proposes update-to-update windows and indicates whether events isolate on the driving path.
questions.answer_full: Slice on your actual update data dates — each monthly update becomes a window, using Update vs Update to measure the critical-path movement and progress per period. That isolates when the +47 wd accrued rather than arguing it globally. Whether events isolate cleanly depends on the driving path staying on the jetty across windows; if it re-routes to the silo mid-analysis, that window needs separate treatment. If events won't isolate per window it defaults toward a weaker global claim. Your consultant sets the final windows.

Which limb applies depends entirely on the actual cause, your contract edition and the Particular Conditions — confirm the exact clause with your contracts manager against the signed contract.

questions.q: How many working days do my calendars give me, and what exceptions — holidays, reduced hours, shutdowns — are in them?
