questions.answer_sketch: Working-days timeline and the exception/working-hours profile.
questions.answer_full: Run the Calendar Audit — it lays out the net working-days timeline per calendar and every exception baked in: public holidays, reduced-hours periods and any imposed shutdown. On a marine job the calendar assigned to the jetty front matters most: pile driving, deck and fender install shouldn't be sitting on a lean 5-day office calendar. Confirm the marine activities carry a proper site calendar with realistic hours and daylight — that's where hidden lost time hides, and where part of the jetty's -18 wd can quietly originate.

questions.q: Compare two calendars — where do they differ?
questions.grounds: Calendar Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Side-by-side calendar comparison of working days and hours.
questions.answer_full: Use the Calendar Audit's side-by-side compare — it shows exactly where two calendars differ in working days and daily hours. The pair to check here is the marine/jetty calendar against your general civil calendar. If the governing jetty front runs on a leaner calendar, that alone can inflate part of the 18 working days it's behind. Reconcile them before you trust any float or the +47 wd finish position — a calendar mismatch on the driving path distorts the whole forecast calculation.

questions.q: How many weather days did we lose this month, and what did it do to the finish?
questions.grounds: Weather Impact
questions.answer_sketch: Lost days and milestone slip for the environmental section of the report.
questions.answer_full: Run the Bad-Weather Impact analysis with the coastal/marine site-type preset — it counts the workable days lost against your weather criteria and carries them through to a forecast-finish effect. Be honest about the split: the jetty is already -18 wd on the governing path and forecast finish sits at ~20 Apr 2027, +47 wd late. Isolate how much of that marine slip is weather versus execution, because only the weather-attributable portion is a time-impact indicator you can put in front of the client — not the whole slip.

questions.q: What's the weather-adjusted finish if weather stays typical for this site, and what recovery offsets the weather days?
questions.grounds: Weather Impact, What-if / scenario engine
questions.answer_sketch: Weather-adjusted finish under a typical year (site-type presets) and the acceleration needed to absorb it.
questions.answer_full: The tool builds a weather-adjusted finish on a typical year for the coastal site type, then you offset it in the what-if engine. Sequence it: start from +47 wd, layer expected marine downtime, then apply the P6-verified levers — jetty night shift recovers ~6 wd, a second piling crew ~4 wd. Those two together only partly cover the pre-weather slip, so weather-adjusted you'll still carry exposure. Time the piling push into the calmer-sea window so the recovery isn't eaten straight back by downtime.

questions.q: How many of the crew-days I'm adding will just be lost to weather anyway?
questions.grounds: Weather Impact, Calendar Audit, Productivity & Resource Intelligence
questions.answer_sketch: Avoids over-resourcing weather-sensitive fronts and times the push for the dry window.
questions.answer_full: Right question to ask before you throw a crew at the jetty. Cross the Weather Impact lost-day profile against the fronts you're accelerating — pile driving and fender install are the most sea-state-sensitive. Add a piling crew (~4 wd P6-verified) through a rough window and a chunk of those crew-days land on non-workable days, so you pay standby for nothing. Push the extra resources into the calm window and keep the night shift for weather-protected deck work. Don't over-man a weather-exposed front.

questions.q: Do my procurement and shipping durations account for holidays and site shutdowns?
questions.grounds: Calendar Audit
questions.answer_sketch: Checks the calendar on procurement activities so lead times aren't optimistic across non-working time.
questions.answer_full: Check it in the Calendar Audit — put the procurement and shipping activities under the lens and confirm the calendar assigned to them, not just the durations. Lead times and sea-freight legs must run on a calendar carrying holidays and any port/site shutdown, or the delivery dates read optimistically. Engineering and procurement are broadly on track here, so don't manufacture a problem — but a fabricated jetty component landing on a shutdown could clip the marine front. Verify the calendar first, then trust the dates.

questions.q: How do I show the shutdown period wasn't my delay?

questions.answer_sketch: Documents imposed shutdown/holiday exceptions so non-working time isn't counted against the contractor.

The Calendar Audit pulls out every imposed shutdown and holiday exception as non-working time already carried in the schedule — those days were never yours to work. Pair that with a Consultant Review before/after run showing the finish position with and without the shutdown window. Keep it factual: this evidences the non-working time is calendar-imposed, not contractor slippage — a time-impact indicator, never an entitlement finding. Present the exceptions and the reconciled dates and let the record speak for itself.
